title: Rethinking Loss Reweighting for Imbalance Learning as an Inverse Problem: A Neural Collapse Point of View
claim: Baseline training leaves classifiers misaligned with minority class means; our method aligns weights with all class means symmetrically.
layout: 2 panels side-by-side, (a) baseline vs (b) ours, toy 2-D scatter
description: Two side-by-side toy 2-D feature-space panels, labeled (a) Baseline and (b) Ours, each with three Gaussian point clouds: a large dense pink majority class, a medium green class, and a tiny sparse blue minority class. Black crosses mark class means. Thick gray lines radiate from a common center as classifier weight vectors, and dashed black lines connect the center to each class mean. In the baseline, the gray classifier vectors are skewed: the pink one aligns with its mean, while the green classifier points off-target and the blue one is misdirected, so the minority classes are poorly aligned. In (b), the three gray vectors lie along the dashed lines to each class mean in a balanced ETF-like Y shape. The eye goes first to the big pink cluster, then to the contrast in gray vector alignment.
caption: Toy examples with 2-dimensional features and 3 classes to illustrate the feature learning of classification. Black crosses are the class means, and gray lines are the classifier weights.
abstract: Loss reweighting is a widely used strategy for long-tailed classification, but existing reweighting strategies often rely on heuristics and rarely define a well-specified target. Inspired by Neural Collapse (NC), the ideal simplex Equiangular Tight Frame (ETF) terminal geometry suggests equal per-class average loss as a reasonable target for reweighting. Based on the ideal equal loss objective, we consider loss reweighting as an inverse problem and propose an inverse-view reweighting strategy that infers class weights dynamically to match this ideal objective. Empirically, NC metrics suggest our method can effectively reduce the loss imbalance coefficient and closer alignment with NC geometry while consistently outperforming strong long-tailed baselines on different datasets.
